newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German coalition slowly narrowing budget gap.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German coalition slowly narrowing budget gap.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition government on Wednesday searched for more cuts to complete its 1997 draft budget after agreeing to put on ice a divisive row over cutting an unpopular tax to rebuild eastern Germany.
Kohl met ministers from his Christian Democrat party (CDU) to seek further savings, and coalition sources said next year's financing gap had been whittled down to three billion marks ($1.9 billion).

But more bargaining will be needed before the budget is finalised early next week, keeping Finance Minister Theo Waigel under intense pressure to produce a credible package to make Germany fit for European monetary union.

Waigel, defending his record against attacks from both within and outside the government, said his ninth budget would meet the Maastricht treaty's strict targets even though there has been a big overshoot in borrowing this year.
"We will be within plan in 1997," he told Stern magazine in an interview to be published on Thursday.

Kohl's coalition appeared at last to be working together after weeks of backbiting which had taken his 14-year alliance with Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU) and the liberal Free Democrats (FDP) close to collapse.
The Kohl-Waigel axis has been hobbled by a tax blockade by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and a refusal by the FDP to allow tax hikes to compensate.
"The tail is wagging the dog. The FDP is succeeding in forcing the CDU/CSU into the most absurd contortions -- and the Chancellor lets it happen," the Sueddeutsche Zeitung commented.

Waigel has pledged to hit the Maastricht treaty's debt and budget deficit limits of 60 percent and three percent of gross domestic product respectively next year. His deficit target of around 60 billion marks next year equals 2.5 percent of GDP.
Those goals underpin Germany's demand for a tough stability pact to enforce budget discipline on countries wanting to join the planned launch of the single European currency in 1999.
After two rounds of talks on Tuesday, the coalition agreed to put back talks on cutting the so-called "solidarity tax" -- a 7.5 percent surcharge on taxes owed -- until mid-December.
The FDP wants a two-point cut in 1998, a demand that Kohl and Waigel are not yet ready to accept.
Waigel is also expected to hold further talks with the SPD -- who can block tax measures in parliament's upper house -- over reforming corporate taxes.
Those negotiations could be tricky, with the SPD keeping up its attacks on Waigel by saying 22 billion marks were missing in his calculations on this year's budget.
"If Waigel can't give any clear information after 11 months of the budget year, he is in the wrong job," SPD budget spokesman Karl Diller said in a statement.

Meanwhile, the coalition will concentrate on readying its 1997 budget by early next week for passage through parliament at the end of November. Sources said the three billion mark gap took account of new tax revenue estimates due on Friday.

FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle, trying to patch up strained coalition relations, said the tax row had been a storm which had helped to clear the air. "I expect that there will be no problems in passing the budget," he told ZDF television.
And, although Waigel hinted in the Stern interview that he may be ready to quit the finance portfolio and take over as foreign minister, that move is regarded as unlikely.
The only alternative to the status quo, the Sueddeutsche Zeitung noted, would be for Kohl to extend his record run as Chancellor at the head of a grand coalition with the SPD.
That is something none of the three ruling parties want. -- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150 ($1=1.5217 Mark)
